findings.summary: In the "Which Tool?" flowchart the edge labels for the q→reflog and q→revert branches are drawn on top of the "cherry-pick" and "bisect" pills, making all four strings illegible.
findings.evidence: The word "recover" sits directly over the green pill reading "cherry-pick" (rendering as "cherry-pick"/"recover" superimposed), and "shared branch" sits over the blue pill reading "bisect", both at roughly y=1030 in slide-02.png; source post.json defines edges {"from":"q","to":"c","label":"recover"} and {"from":"q","to":"d","label":"shared branch"}.
findings.fix: Route the q→c and q→d edges so their labels are placed on the long vertical segments below the first-row pills (or give the flow four columns / a second rank) so no edge label is painted over a node; alternatively drop the labels on those two edges.

findings.summary: The caption's first sentence is a series label rather than a hook, burying the actual hook in sentence two.
findings.evidence: "Part 2 of GIT TIME TRAVEL. Git never really deletes your work — you just lose the pointer to it."
findings.fix: Lead with the hook and demote the series marker: "Git never really deletes your work — you just lose the pointer to it. Part 2 of GIT TIME TRAVEL is a field guide to the three tools that get it back..."

findings.summary: The page opens with "5. Worked Example" before sections 2–4, so it uses `git cherry` and patch-id matching several blocks before the section that introduces them.
findings.evidence: First block is `{"type":"heading","text":"5. Worked Example"}` whose bullets/code read "Patch-id drops only __byte-identical__ ones" and "git cherry -v main rel-2.4 / # '+' = still unmerged upstream", while the block that explains the command — "2. Find What To Pick" with note "`git cherry` matches by patch-id" and "'+' = unmerged, '-' = already in" — comes after it.
findings.fix: Move the "Worked Example" block to after "2. Find What To Pick" (or to the end of the page) so the numbered sections run 2 → 3 → 4 → 5 → 6 and `git cherry`/patch-id are introduced before the example that relies on them.

findings.summary: The destructive-triad table says `reset --hard` destroys the working tree and index yet is fully recoverable via reflog, but the reflog only records ref movements, so uncommitted tree/index changes it discards are gone.
findings.fix: Split the guarantee: change the cell to something like "**commits** yes via reflog — **uncommitted tree/index changes: no**" (staged blobs are recoverable only via `git fsck --lost-found`).

findings.summary: The destructive-triad table asserts `reset --hard` is recoverable via reflog with no qualification, but the reflog only recovers committed work — the uncommitted tree and index it also destroys are gone.
findings.evidence: Row: ["`reset --hard`","tree + index + HEAD","**yes** via reflog"] — the row itself names "tree + index" as destroyed yet answers the recoverability column with an unqualified "**yes** via reflog".
findings.fix: Qualify the cell, e.g. "**HEAD only** — via reflog", and add a line under the table: "The reflog stores ref movements, not working-tree state — changes you never committed or stashed are not recoverable by any of these."

findings.summary: The worked example claims patch-id only matches byte-identical patches, but `git patch-id` ignores line numbers and (outside `--verbatim`) whitespace, so cherry-picks that landed at a different offset still match.
findings.evidence: "Patch-id drops only __byte-identical__ ones; conflict-resolved picks stay"
findings.fix: Reword to "Patch-id ignores line numbers and whitespace, so cleanly applied picks drop out; only conflict-resolved (content-changed) picks stay".

findings.summary: The example asserts `git merge main` re-offers all 14 cherry-picked patches, but a three-way merge silently coalesces changes that are identical on both sides — only picks whose resolution differed actually re-surface.
findings.fix: Change to "`git merge main` replays all 14 from main's side — identical ones merge silently, conflict-resolved ones come back as conflicts".
